AD 30–70 · Earliest years

Guiding questions
  • What happened after Jesus' death?
  • How did the apostles organize communities?
  • Where, how often, and how did Christians gather and worship?
  • How does the Eucharist relate historically to the Last Supper?
  • What did Peter, James, John, Paul and others do?
  • What happened as the apostles died?

Surviving narrative and letters for this generation are almost entirely canonical New Testament texts. External notices are brief and later copied. Silence is not evidence.

Meanwhile in the world
after 30 BCE

Egypt: decades after Cleopatra’s death (30 BCE), Egypt is a Roman province — the movie Cleopatra era is already over.

source
41–54

Rome: Claudius is emperor; Rome invades Britain in 43 (the start of Roman Britain).

source
25–220

China: Eastern (Later) Han dynasty rules from Luoyang — a global anchor far from the Mediterranean.

source
54–68

Rome: Nero is emperor — the villain of countless movies and novels about Rome.

source
60 or 61

Britain: Boudica (Boudicca) leads the Iceni revolt against Rome — Warrior Queen territory.

source
64 legend

Rome: Great Fire of Rome under Nero (the “fiddled while Rome burned” story is later legend).

source
66–70

Judaea: First Jewish Revolt; Titus takes Jerusalem and destroys the Second Temple in 70.

source
c. 1–100

Mexico: Teotihuacán growing into a major city — pyramids rising while Nero rules Rome.

source

Evidence shows: New Testament texts that Christians preserved as scripture describe early Jerusalem and diaspora communities, a shared meal tradition, and named leaders; Josephus mentions James; Roman historians mention Christians in connection with Rome under Nero and Claudius.

Historians infer: Frequency of gatherings, exact local variety of meal practice, and day-to-day organization beyond what the texts happen to mention.

Still unknown: The full sequence of events after many apostles' deaths; most local community records; nearly all liturgical detail outside a few New Testament passages.

AD 70–150 · After the apostles

Guiding questions
  • How was apostolic teaching transmitted?
  • Who led afterward?
  • What about bishops, presbyters, and deacons?
  • What did ordinary Christian life, prayer, baptism, and Sunday worship look like?
  • How did churches communicate and stay united?
  • What did Christians believe before the later councils?

This is the densest surviving Christian letter-and-manual layer after the New Testament. Many texts traditionally linked to the apostles belong here.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

Pompeii dies, Colosseum opens — within a year

Vesuvius buries Pompeii in 79; Titus inaugurates the Colosseum with games in 80 — both just after the apostles’ generation.

source

Cai Lun’s paper and Ignatius/Trajan

Around Ignatius’s letters (c. 107–110) and Pliny–Trajan (c. 112), Cai Lun was at the Eastern Han court; he reported improved papermaking c. 105.

source · source

source

Rome: Colosseum inaugurated with games — gladiators for real, not just in movies.

source
98–117

Rome: Trajan emperor; the empire reaches its widest eastern extent.

source
c. 105

China: Cai Lun reports improved papermaking to the Eastern Han court.

source

Rome: Hadrian; Hadrian’s Wall begun in Britain (122s) — still walkable today.

source

China: Eastern Han continues; Luoyang among the world’s largest cities.

source

Mexico: Teotihuacán rising — pyramids of the Sun and Moon taking shape.

source

Evidence shows: Letters from Rome, Antioch, and Smyrna; a church-order manual (Didache); an early martyr narrative for Polycarp; Pliny's provincial procedure under Trajan.

Historians infer: How universal any one local pattern was; exact authorship of anonymous works.

Still unknown: Most local archives; full biographies of most leaders; whether some manuals describe ideal or actual practice.

AD 150–325 · Developing Church

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass and the sacraments take shape?
  • How was doctrine becoming defined?
  • What controversies arose?
  • What effects did persecution have?
  • What was the role of Rome and other churches?
  • How were authoritative writings determined?

From Justin's ritual descriptions through Irenaeus and the African and Latin writers to Eusebius and Nicaea, this period has the richest primary documentation for worship, conflict, and canon.

Meanwhile in the world
161–180

Rome: Marcus Aurelius emperor — the philosopher-emperor; his son Commodus is the villain of the film Gladiator.

source
c. 166

China–Rome contact: a reported envoy from Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court.

source
220

China: Han dynasty ends; Three Kingdoms period begins (220–265) — the era of countless East Asian novels and games.

source
224–241

Persia: Ardashīr I founds the Sasanian empire, ending Parthian rule.

source
235–284

Rome: Crisis of the Third Century — emperors rise and fall in rapid succession.

source
c. 200+

Mexico: Teotihuacán a major urban centre (Temple of Quetzalcóatl graves ~200 CE).

source
3rd–4th c.

Africa: Kingdom of Aksum rising as a Red Sea trading power.

source
313

Rome: Edict of Milan — Constantine and Licinius grant toleration for Christianity.

source
325

Nicaea: First Council of Nicaea under Constantine.

source

Evidence shows: Second-century apologies and church manuals; named controversies (Marcion, Gnostic teachers, Quartodeciman Pascha dispute, rebaptism); martyr acts; third-century unity and baptism debates; early fourth-century imperial shift in Lactantius and Eusebius; Nicaea creed and canons.

Historians infer: How typical any one city's liturgy was; motives in polemical sources.

Still unknown: Full texts of many opponents (often known only through critics); exact authorship of some church orders.

Church History

Eusebius of Caesarea

c. 312–324 Other early Christian
ⓘ Read with care

Eusebius is the key early Church historian, but he is not a saint in the West and for a time sympathized with Arius before accepting the Creed at Nicaea.

Documentary church history (including canon notes in HE 3.25 and the Pascha dispute in HE 5.23–25). New Advent index to the ten books (tr. McGiffert, NPNF 2.1).

🌍 Constantine after Milvian Bridge (312) and Milan (313); Sasanian Persia. source

AD 325–1000 · After Constantine

Guiding questions
  • What changed after Constantine?
  • How did buildings, liturgy, vestments, art, and music develop?
  • Which councils clarified teaching?
  • How did monasticism grow?
  • How did East and West diverge?
  • Which early practices survived or changed?

Selective coverage. Favor documents that show practice (Egeria, Cyril's mystagogical lectures, Apostolic Constitutions 8, monastic rules) and the great Christological and creedal councils, plus II Nicaea on images.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

Chalcedon and Attila — same year

Council of Chalcedon (451) is the same year a Roman–Visigoth force checked Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

source · source

Augustine writing while Maya Classic cities rose

Confessions (c. 397–400) and City of God (413–426) overlap the Maya Classic Period (c. 250–900), when Tikal and other cities flourished.

source

Benedict’s Rule and the Arthur legend-setting legend

Benedict’s Rule (c. 530) falls in the post-Roman British centuries where later Arthurian legends are set — Arthur himself is legend, not verified history.

source · source

early 4th–late 6th c.

India: Gupta dynasty — a classical age of literature, math, and art.

source
c. 250–900

Mesoamerica: Maya Classic Period — Tikal, Palenque, Copán (the cities in every Maya documentary).

source
476

West: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus — conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.

source
527–565

Byzantium: Justinian I; Hagia Sophia built.

source
618–907

China: Tang dynasty — often called a golden age of Chinese culture.

source
793

England: Vikings raid Lindisfarne — the attack that opens every Viking Age story.

source
800–814

Europe: Charlemagne crowned emperor of the Romans (800); dies 814.

source
622

Arabia: Hijrah — Muhammad migrates from Mecca to Medina; start of the Muslim era.

source

Evidence shows: Imperial patronage narratives; catechetical and liturgical descriptions; monastic rules; conciliar definitions; pilgrim observation of Jerusalem rites.

Historians infer: How quickly local rites converged; how representative one pilgrim or one rule was.

Still unknown: Continuous musical notation for earliest chant; many ceremonial details before later Ordines.

AD 1000–present · Medieval Church onward

Guiding questions
  • How did the Mass reach recognizable forms?
  • How did spirituality, theology, and devotion develop?
  • Which modern Catholic traditions trace early, and which arose later?

Selective milestones: a short spine of Mass and doctrine documents alongside spiritual classics. These establish official teaching at dated moments; they do not by themselves prove day-to-day parish practice.

Meanwhile in the world

✦ Fun overlaps

1066 still sits on today’s British throne

William wins at Hastings (1066). From his granddaughter Matilda’s son Henry II onward, every English (then British) monarch descends from William — including Charles III.

source · source · source

Teresa of Ávila and Elizabeth I

Teresa’s Life (1565) and Interior Castle (1577) fall squarely in Elizabeth I’s reign (1558–1603) — rival Catholic and Protestant worlds, same decades.

source · source

Shakespeare and Galileo, born the year before Teresa’s Life

Shakespeare baptized 1564; Galileo born 1564 — the year before Teresa’s Life (1565). Both alive through Quo Primum, Interior Castle, and John of the Cross’s 1580s works.

source · source · source

Devout Life while Jamestown and Pocahontas’s world open

Francis de Sales’s Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) lands two years after Jamestown (1607), in the Pocahontas era — and the same years Galileo is turning his telescope on the sky.

source · source

Lateran IV and Magna Carta — same year

Fourth Lateran Council canons and Magna Carta are both dated 1215.

source

Joan of Arc’s lifetime overlaps The Imitation of Christ

Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431) is alive across the window usually given for The Imitation of Christ (c. 1418–27).

source

Cahokia a mega-city while Aquinas writes the Summa

Cahokia near today’s St. Louis flourished c. 950–1350 (up to ~20,000 people) — still a major centre when Aquinas wrote the Summa (1265–74) and when Lateran IV met (1215).

source · source

Mansa Musa’s gold hajj before Catherine of Siena

Mansa Musa’s spectacular pilgrimage (1324) is only about fifty years before Catherine’s Dialogue (1377–78).

source · source

Thérèse’s 1890s — baseball already America’s pastime legend

By Story of a Soul (1895–97), baseball was established in the U.S. The Abner Doubleday “invented it in 1839” story is legend, not history.

source · source

Culloden (Outlander) sits between two Deep Dive books

No Deep Dive writing is from 1746, but Culloden — the last Jacobite battle — falls in the long gap between Introduction to the Devout Life (1609) and Story of a Soul (1895–97).

source

c. 950–1350

North America: Cahokia (near today’s St. Louis) flourishes — up to ~20,000 people; largest city north of Mexico before Europeans. (Pre-contact Cherokee politics are mostly unknown from written sources.)

source
1206–27

Asia: Genghis Khan builds the Mongol empire — the conqueror from every world-history classroom.

source
1324

West Africa: Mansa Musa’s gold-laden pilgrimage to Mecca makes Mali famous across the Mediterranean.

source
1412?–31

France: Joan of Arc leads French forces, then is executed (1431) — the Maid of Orléans of stage and screen.

source
c. 1455

Germany: Gutenberg completes his 42-line Bible — movable type that changes Europe.

source
1492 / 1519–21

Atlantic & Mexico: Columbus reaches the Caribbean (1492); Cortés and allies take Tenochtitlán (1521), ending Aztec imperial rule.

source
1509–47

England: Henry VIII reigns — and his six wives become schoolroom legend.

source
1558–1603

England: Elizabeth I; Shakespeare baptized 1564 and Galileo born 1564 — the Tudor/Armada world of film and novels.

source
1607–14 / 1746

Virginia: Jamestown founded 1607; Pocahontas era. Scotland: Culloden 1746 ends the Jacobite rising (Outlander territory) — between Devout Life and Story of a Soul.

source

Evidence shows: Official teaching and rubrical policy at dated moments (councils, papal constitutions, spiritual classics).

Historians infer: Continuity claims with the earliest centuries are historical judgments, not automatic from the texts.

Still unknown: How every parish practiced day to day between these milestones.
